## Claims — grouped by pericope

### 6:18–20 (Persevering in Watchful Prayer)

- **[6:18]** The section is grammatically tied to 6:10–20 but thematically new; military
  imagery drops away. Thielman: "The military imagery largely disappears, and Paul now
  focuses on a straightforward appeal to his readers to devote themselves to prayer for
  all believers, and especially for him." (line 10) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:18]** Two participles govern: *proseuchomenoi* (praying) and *agrypnountes*
  (being watchful). Syntax debated: some put a period at 6:17 → read imperatively
  (precedent Rom. 12:9–21, citing Sellin 2008). Thielman prefers attaching them loosely
  to the imperative *dexasthe* (receive, 6:17), paralleling *hypotassomenoi* (submitting,
  5:21) relative to *plērousthe* (5:18): "these participles adopt an independent,
  imperatival quality of their own." (lines 20–28) — *Thielman* (with Robertson 1923,
  Wallace 1996, Fee 1994, Hoehner 2002).
- **[6:18]** Prayer should have **five characteristics**: constant, Spirit-empowered,
  alert/watchful, zealous in devotion, and ecumenical in breadth. "Paul urges his readers
  to defend their position in Christ against the onslaught of evil by prayer that is
  constant, Spirit-empowered, alert to surrounding evil, zealous in its devotion, and
  ecumenical in its breadth." (line 40) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:18]** "pray in the Spirit" (*en pneumati*) = prayer the Spirit **empowers**, not
  merely "in the sphere of the Spirit" or heartfelt prayer: "prayer that the Spirit has
  given the believer the strength to utter." (line 32) — *Thielman* (contra Eadie 1883,
  Heil 2007a, Westcott 1906; with Fee 1994, citing Rom. 8:26).
- **[6:18]** *agrypneō* = "lie awake, pass sleepless nights" (LSJ), used in early
  Christian eschatological contexts (Mark 13:33; Luke 21:34–36) for staying awake for the
  Son of Man's coming. (line 34) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:18]** *proskarterēsis* (devotion/perseverance) is a rare word, before Ephesians
  appearing only twice: a 2nd-c.-BC Andros inscription and the 1st-c.-BC philosopher
  Philodemus. The Andros inscription describes an admired physician who "gave himself
  over" (*epedōken heauton*) to his profession with "particular devotion"
  (*proskarterēsis*); Paul urges the zeal "normally associated with the committed
  practice of a craft or trade." (line 36) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:19–20]** Paul asks prayer for himself because as a prisoner in a "chain" (*halysis*)
  facing a legal hearing he is tempted to soften or omit politically sensitive elements of
  the gospel. (line 44) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:20]** Paul "serves as an ambassador" (*presbeuō*; cf. 2 Cor. 5:20). An ambassador
  in the eastern Roman Empire "was charged with traveling to a specific destination for
  the purpose of communicating the interests of another party to those in power." (line 46,
  citing Bash 1997) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:19]** He asks for *parrēsia* / *parrēsiazomai* (boldness) — divinely inspired,
  candid speech "especially in the presence of powerful people" (Let. Aris. 125; Acts
  4:13, 29; Josephus). Scripture describes God "opening the mouth" of his spokesperson
  (Exod. 4:12 LXX etc.). (line 48) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:19]** "the mystery of the gospel" (*to mystērion tou euangeliou*) = the mystery
  defined earlier: Jews and Gentiles united in Christ's body (3:3–6), part of a cosmic
  unity embracing "all rule and authority and power and lordship" (1:21). "This may have
  been precisely the element of the mystery that Paul was tempted to leave out of any
  testimony before a government official." (line 50) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:19 Additional Note, textual]** *tou euangeliou* is omitted by B (Vat.), F, G, some
  Old Latin, Victorinus, Ambrosiaster, but has strong Alexandrian (א, A, I, Ψ, 33, 1739),
  Western (D), and Byzantine support. Thielman (with Metzger 1994) judges the longer
  reading *to mystērion tou euangeliou* probably original. (line 62) — *Thielman/Metzger.*
- **[6:20 Additional Note, textual]** Witnesses vary between *en autō* after
  *parrēsiasōmai*, and the simple accusative *auto* (𝔓46, B, 1739, 1881). Thielman
  judges *en autō parrēsiasōmai* likely correct on broad-spread testimony (A, I, Ψ, 6, 33,
  81; D, F, G; most Byzantine); "the meaning 'with respect to it, I might speak boldly'
  remains unaffected." (line 64) — *Thielman/Metzger, Best 1998.*

### 6:21–22 (Tychicus)

- **[6:21–22]** Tychicus is the letter's implied courier, sent both to report Paul's
  circumstances and to encourage the readers (discouraged per 3:13 by Paul's suffering).
  (lines 81, 106) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:21–22]** Remarkable redundancy: three phrases for Paul's circumstances —
  *ta kat' eme* (my circumstances), *ti prassō* (how I am doing), *ta peri hēmōn* (our
  circumstances). The plural "our" probably refers to Paul and Tychicus (Best 1998).
  "the redundancy probably emphasizes how full Tychicus's account... will be." (line 116)
  — *Thielman.*
- **[6:21–22]** Tychicus commended with two phrases: "beloved brother" (*agapētos
  adelphos*, also of Onesimus, Philem. 16) and "faithful servant [*diakonos*] in the
  Lord." *diakonos* here carries the "menial service" sense of courier/assistant (BDAG),
  though it could denote church office elsewhere (Phil. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3). (lines 118–120)
  — *Thielman.*
- **[6:21–22]** Other NT data on Tychicus: representative from Asia for the Jerusalem
  collection (Acts 20:4); carried Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon to Colossae
  (Col. 4:7–9); later possibly sent to Crete (Titus 3:12) and again to Ephesus (2 Tim.
  4:12). (line 120) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:21–22]** Ancient letter-carrying context: no public postal service for private
  use; reliable couriers were scarce. Cicero to Atticus: "I have been slow about sending
  one... for lack of a safe messenger... very few... can carry a letter of weight without
  lightening it by perusal" (Att. 1.13, cited via Richards 2004). Paul assures readers
  "the contents are safe with Tychicus." (line 122) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:21 Additional Note]** On *kai* in *kai hymeis* ("you too"): options canvassed —
  Paul himself as referent (Alford, Schnackenburg), churches on Tychicus's itinerary /
  Colossae (Robinson, Haupt, Hoehner), or imprecise usage (Lincoln, Best). Thielman's
  preferred reading (giving *kai* its normal force): Tychicus carried Ephesians **and**
  Colossians and Philemon, so readers know he was also charged with informing the
  Colossians. **AUTHORSHIP-RELEVANT:** Sellin (2008), holding Ephesians pseudonymous,
  reads the *kai* the same way but as part of the pseudonymous author's verisimilitude
  strategy; Thielman: "It is equally plausible... to take the air of reality created by
  this small detail as evidence that both Ephesians and Colossians are genuine epistles of
  Paul, composed at about the same time and dispatched with Tychicus." (lines 132–134)
  — *positions recorded; Thielman favors authenticity.*

### 6:23–24 (Peace, Love, Faith, Grace — double prayer-wish)

- **[6:23–24]** The conclusion follows a standard Pauline pattern: prayer request for
  self, courier's travel plans, peace prayer-wish, and (in all letters) a grace prayer-wish.
  (lines 83–85) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:23–24] TWO UNIQUE FEATURES (authorship-relevant):**
  1. Both prayer-wishes are **third person** ("Peace to the brothers... Grace be with all
     those who love..."), whereas Pauline peace-wishes are normally second person (Gal.
     6:16 excepted) and grace-wishes **always** second person. Thielman: "probably yet
     another sign that the letter was intended for all the Christians in the various house
     churches in Ephesus, many of whom Paul did not know personally after his nearly
     seven-year absence." (line 87) — *Thielman.*
  2. Most of 6:21 and all of 6:22 **duplicate Col. 4:7–8 word for word** — "twenty-nine
     consecutive words" (Mitton 1951), differing only by *kai syndoulos* (and fellow slave)
     in Col. 4:7. "The most reasonable explanation... is that the author of one letter—or
     his secretary—had before him, and copied out, the words of the other letter" (Lincoln
     1990; Mitton; Sellin). Not unprecedented: Ignatius gave an identical commendation of
     courier Burrhus in two letters (Ign. Phld. 11.2; Ign. Smyrn. 12.1). Thielman's
     explanation: Paul sent Ephesians, Colossians, Philemon with Tychicus; after composing
     Tychicus's commendation for Colossians, "instructed his secretary to repeat them in
     Ephesians... with a few, probably unconscious, changes." (line 89) — *positions
     recorded; Thielman favors authenticity via same-occasion composition.*
- **[6:23]** "peace" (*eirēnē*) recalls the letter's developed sense: Christ is "peace"
  who abolished the Mosaic law's dividing wall (2:14–18), peace as "fastener" of church
  unity (4:3), "the gospel of peace" (6:15). (line 161) — *Thielman.* [Only reference to
  armor-section material 6:15 in this slice.]
- **[6:23]** "brothers [and sisters]" (*hoi adelphoi*): Jewish usage for fellow Jews
  (Deut. 18:15 etc.); Jesus redefined it for those doing God's will (Mark 3:33–35); Paul
  uses *adelphos* figuratively more than any NT author (130×), and can expand the figure
  (self as "mother"/"father," Jesus as "brother," Rom. 8:29). Heavy familial language may
  reflect converts' alienation from families/society (Malherbe 2000). (lines 163–165)
  — *Thielman.*
- **[6:23]** "love with faith" (*agapē meta pisteōs*): faith is syntactically subordinate,
  but given the letter's linking of love and faith (1:15; 3:17) one shouldn't overpress it.
  Both love and faith are major letter themes; the prayer is that knowledge of God's love
  "might flourish in the fertile soil of their faith in the gospel." (lines 151, 167)
  — *Thielman.*
- **[6:23]** Peace, love, and faith come "from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" —
  even the human virtues are, if the prayer is answered, gifts of God (cf. 1:2). (line 169)
  — *Thielman.*
- **[6:24]** Every Pauline letter ends with a grace prayer-wish; later letters simply ask
  "grace be with" the readers (Col. 4:18; Eph. 6:24; 1 Tim. 6:21; Titus 3:15; 2 Tim.
  4:22). (line 171) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:24]** Only 2 Cor. 13:13 and Eph. 6:24 vary the pattern widely, differently. Eph.
  6:24 shifts the grace-of-Christ reference into the description of recipients: "all those
  who love our Lord Jesus Christ incorruptibly" — the most elaborate recipient description
  in the corpus. Positive counterpart to 1 Cor. 16:22 ("If anyone does not love the Lord,
  let him be accursed"). The obligation to love God is prominent in OT/NT (Deut. 6:5 etc.)
  and Second Temple Jewish literature (Sir., Pss. Sol., Testaments). (lines 173–175)
  — *Thielman.*
- **[6:24]** *en aphtharsia* ("in incorruption/immortality") is a genuine crux —
  "has left interpreters puzzled" (Sellin 2008). *aphtharsia* = "incorruptibility,
  immortality" (BDAG), with a long Greek-philosophical history (eternity of God, soul,
  world) and Hellenistic-Jewish uses (Wis. 2:23; 4 Macc. 9:22; 17:12; contrasted with
  mortality in 1 Cor. 15). (line 177) — *Thielman.* See dedicated section below.

## Tychicus & closing (6:21–24) — detail

Covered fully above. Key authorship-load-bearing points consolidated:

1. **Col 4:7–8 verbatim overlap** (line 89): 29 consecutive identical words across Eph.
   6:21–22 and Col. 4:7–8 (minus *kai syndoulos*). Thielman: same-occasion composition by
   Paul/secretary copying the Colossians commendation into Ephesians. Cited: Mitton 1951:
   59; Lincoln 1990: lv; Sellin 2008: 490; Ignatius parallel (courier Burrhus). This is
   the central data point tying Ephesians–Colossians literary relationship to the
   authorship debate; positions preserved without adjudication, though Thielman argues for
   authenticity.
2. **Third-person prayer-wishes** (line 87): unusual for Paul; Thielman reads as a sign of
   an impersonal, circular letter to Ephesian house churches Paul did not personally know
   (seven-year absence) — not as evidence of pseudonymity.
3. **The *kai hymeis* argument** (line 134): Sellin (pseudonymist) vs. Thielman
   (authenticity), both from the same exegetical datum.

## The *en aphtharsia* crux (6:24) — interpretive options

Thielman canvasses solutions for "love the Lord Jesus Christ *en aphtharsia*":
1. **Unceasing/persistent love** (Hoehner 2002; Best 1998) — Thielman: not an obvious
   translation of *aphtharsia*. (line 181)
2. **Rhetorical flourish for the whole sentence** — believers exist in the realm of
   "immortality" (raised/seated with Christ, 2:5–6) (Heil 2007a; cf. Barth 1974; Sellin).
   Preserves the word's meaning but sacrifices the obvious syntax. (line 183)
3. **Attach *en* to *charis* ("grace and immortality")**, taking *en* as a connective
   (Bruce 1984; Lincoln 1990). Intelligible, but *en aphtharsia* sits too far from
   *charis*. (line 185)
4. **Thielman's own solution** (lines 187–271): compare the structure to **Psalms of
   Solomon 6.6**, a liturgical formula. Parallel table (lines 189–235):
   - Pss. Sol. 6.6: *hē charis... tois agapōsin auton **en alētheia*** ("...to those who
     love him **in truth**")
   - Eph. 6:24: *hē charis... tōn agapōntōn ton kyrion hēmōn Iēsoun Christon **en
     aphtharsia*** ("...those who love our Lord Jesus Christ **in incorruption**")
   Same structure: abstract divine quality (mercy/grace) → "those who love" the Lord →
   two-word anarthrous *en* + abstract noun (truth/incorruption). A known liturgical
   phrase (also Pss. Sol. 4.25; 10.3; 14.1). Therefore *en aphtharsia* attaches to "those
   who love," and *aphtharsia* is a **virtue** like truth — "in integrity" or "sincerely,"
   not an eternal state. (lines 237–269) — *Thielman.*
   - **Patristic/reception support:** Origen (Cels. 3.60) still saw immortality but read a
     *moral* incorruption (via Heine 2002); Ignatius used the term for moral/doctrinal
     incorruption (Eph. 16.1–17.1; Magn. 6.2; Lightfoot 1890; Moule 1953); NT *aphthartos*
     has moral+temporal sense in 1 Pet. 1:4; 3:4. (line 271) — *Thielman.*
   - **Conclusion:** Paul prays God's grace on those whose love is "free from every element
     liable to corruption" (Westcott 1906); NOT an "eleventh-hour condition of perfect
     love" contradicting 2:1–10, but an implicit admonition to love Christ "simply and
     purely." (line 273) — *Thielman.*
- **[6:24 Additional Note, textual]** Final *amēn* omitted by early, geographically broad
  witnesses (𝔓46, א, A, B, 33, 81, 1175, 1739; F, G) → probably not original; only
  Galatians and Romans seem to have ended with *amēn* (Best 1998); likely crept in via
  liturgical reading (Metzger 1994). (line 283) — *Thielman/Metzger.*

## Named scholars / positions cited

- **Sellin (2008)** — holds Ephesians **pseudonymous**; reads *kai hymeis* (6:21) and the
  Col-parallel as verisimilitude strategy; notes *en aphtharsia* as puzzling. (lines 20,
  89, 132–134, 177, 183, 185, 194 area)
- **Lincoln (1990)** — Col 4:7–8 copying; *kai* imprecise; peace theme; *en aphtharsia*
  connective option; *amēn*. (lines 89, 132, 161, 185)
- **Mitton (1951: 59)** — the "twenty-nine consecutive words" statistic for Eph.
  6:21–22 // Col. 4:7–8. (line 89)
- **Best (1998)** — "our circumstances" = Paul + Tychicus; *kai* imprecise; *aphtharsia*
  = persistent love; *amēn* omission; textual notes. (lines 116, 132, 181, 283)
- **Hoehner (2002)** — syntax of participles; *kai* = Colossae; *aphtharsia* = unceasing;
  love-of-God parallels. (lines 22, 132, 175, 181)
- **Fee (1994)** — participles → *dexasthe*; "in the Spirit" = Spirit-empowered prayer.
  (lines 22, 32)
- **Robertson (1923: 1134)** / **Wallace (1996: 650)** — participle-to-finite-verb rule.
  (line 22)
- **Metzger (1994)** — textual judgments on 6:19, 6:20, 6:24 *amēn*. (lines 62, 64, 283)
- **Heil (2007a)** — "in the sphere of the Spirit" (rejected); *aphtharsia* as realm of
  immortality (option 2). (lines 32, 183)
- **Bash (1997: 4)** — ancient ambassador role. (line 46)
- **Richards (2004: 177–82)** / **Head (2009)** — ancient letter-carriers; Cicero. (line 122)
- **Origen (Cels. 3.60)** via **Heine (2002)** — moral reading of *aphtharsia*. (line 271)
- **Ignatius** (Phld. 11.2; Smyrn. 12.1 — Burrhus; Eph. 16.1–17.1; Magn. 6.2 —
  incorruption). (lines 89, 271)
- **Westcott (1906)** — "spirited" prayer (rejected); "free from every element liable to
  corruption." (lines 32, 273)
- Others cited in passing: Eadie 1883, Alford 1857, Schnackenburg 1991, Robinson 1904,
  Haupt 1902a, Gnilka 1971, Barth 1974, Bruce 1984, Malherbe 2000, Lightfoot 1890, Moule
  1953, Aletti 2001, Philodemus, Josephus, Cicero.

## Notable Greek terms with glosses (as given in slice)

- *dexasthe* — "receive" (imperative, 6:17) — main verb governing 6:18 participles
- *proseuchomenoi* — "praying" (6:18)
- *agrypnountes* / *agrypneō* / *agrypneite* — "being watchful" / "lie awake, pass
  sleepless nights" (6:18)
- *dia pasēs proseuchēs kai deēseōs* — "through every prayer and urgent petition" (6:18)
- *en panti kairō* — "at all times" (6:18)
- *en pneumati* — "in the Spirit" (6:18)
- *eis auto* — "for this purpose" (6:18)
- *proskarterēsis* — devotion/perseverance; rare word (6:18)
- *deēsis* — "urgent petition" (6:18)
- *peri pantōn tōn hagiōn* — "for all the saints" (6:18)
- *halysis* — "chain" (6:20)
- *presbeuō* — "serve as an ambassador" (6:20)
- *parrēsia* / *parrēsiazomai* — "boldness" / "speak boldly" (6:19–20)
- *to mystērion tou euangeliou* — "the mystery of the gospel" (6:19)
- *ta kat' eme* — "my circumstances" (6:21)
- *ti prassō* — "how I am doing" (6:21)
- *ta peri hēmōn* — "our circumstances" (6:22)
- *agapētos adelphos* — "beloved brother" (6:21)
- *diakonos* — "servant/courier/assistant" (6:21)
- *eirēnē* — "peace" (6:23)
- *hoi adelphoi* / *adelphos* — "the brothers [and sisters]" (6:23)
- *agapē meta pisteōs* — "love with faith" (6:23)
- *charis* — "grace" (6:24)
- *tōn agapōntōn* — "those who love" (6:24)
- *en aphtharsia* / *aphtharsia* / *aphthartos* — "in incorruption" / "incorruptibility,
  immortality" / "incorruptible" (6:24) — the closing crux
- *amēn* — textual variant, final word (6:24)

**Terms the brief flagged for special care but which do NOT appear in this slice:**
panoplia, kosmokratores, ta pneumatika tēs ponērias, hē machaira tou pneumatos (all
belong to 6:10–17, absent here).
